blocks.html:
In Short
  • What I Owned: Paper prototypes, the randomized recipe system, the score system, puzzle difficulty progression, and UX and usability tests.
  • Hardest Problems: First, players couldn't read the score; then, they found a speedrun exploit that stopped them talking. Each needed a different kind of fix.
  • What it Shows: Systems validated on paper before engine work, and fixing incentives instead of just blocking exploits.

• Communication Games Overwhelm Easily: Too much information and players shout over each other; too little and the game is trivial.

• Random recipes had to stay fair and comparable between runs.

• 2, 3 or 4 players had to get a balanced challenge from the same levels.

• A small team, so engine time was precious and systems had to be right before building.

1. Talking is the Mechanic. Every system should make players need each other.

2. Hard to Say, not Hard to do. Challenge comes from describing, remembering and coordinating, not from dexterity.

3. The Score Teaches. Players should see how their play turns into points.
I mapped and tested every system interaction on paper and in Miro before anything was built in Unreal. The score was validated first, because every other system feeds into it.

blocks.caption: Every system was proven on paper before it reached Unreal

blocks.html: Recipes are randomized, so the game can't be memorized. To keep scoring fair, every recipe step has a label (type of cut, hot or cold, and so on), each label is worth a fixed number of points, and the total is multiplied by the time left. The system scales for 2, 3 or 4 players.

terms.label: Label Points
terms.note: Fixed per step: cut, hot or cold

terms.label: Dish Score
terms.note: Added up per level, scaled for 2 to 4

blocks.note: Very fast deliveries are quietly damped

blocks.html:
• Problem: Early playtesters couldn't connect what they did with the score they got.
  • Cause: The score was calculated correctly but shown only as a final number, with no sign of what earned it.
  • Fix: I rebalanced the score weights in a feedback spreadsheet, turned secondary objectives into visible bonus multipliers, and tied performance directly to time left.
  • Result: Teams immediately saw how leftover time turned into bonus points for each dish.

• Problem: Players found that delivering very fast made the multiplier shoot up, so they rushed and stopped communicating, which is the opposite of the game's goal.
  • Cause: The time multiplier rewarded speed with no upper limit, so rushing beat talking.
  • Options: Blocking fast deliveries outright would feel like a punishment and tell players they'd found a hole. Changing the incentive was better.
  • Fix: A hidden damping on very fast deliveries that players don't notice, plus a new mechanic where players fix problems around the ship during a level.
  • Result: Speedrunning stopped paying off, and the repair tasks gave players new reasons to talk.
Instead of mechanical locks, each puzzle is built around one of three human limits. Each limit becomes a reason to talk, which is the point of the game.

blocks.caption: Each puzzle turns a human limit into a reason to talk

blocks.html:
• Describing: Dense, similar-looking symbols that partners have to describe precisely to each other.

• Remembering: Information passed between players in sequence under time pressure, before it resets.

• Coordinating: Separated interactions that players must time together by talking, while also moving around.

I co-designed the puzzles with game and level design, and designed the difficulty progression for the recipe and icon puzzles.

I ran closed and open playtests, including at live events, owned the UX process, and ran usability tests. After each delivery, I analysed the playtests and presented adjustments to the team. I also worked with art and UI on readability, and with engineering on the 3C.

blocks.html:
• Hidden damping over a hard rule. A visible speed cap would have told players they'd found a hole; quiet damping kept the game feeling fair.

• Paper before engine. Slower to see anything on screen, but the score and puzzles were already proven when engineering started.

• Fixed label points over per-recipe scores. Less hand-tuning per recipe, but every random recipe scores fairly.

What Worked: Validating the score on paper first, and fixing incentives rather than blocking exploits.

What I'd do Differently: Show the score breakdown from the first prototype, since it caused the first big issue.

What I Learned: A score system is also a teaching tool; if players can't read it, it can't shape how they play. When players find an exploit, ask what it says about the incentives.
